questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical understanding of Kubernetes security primitives including RBAC, ServiceAccount isolation, PodSecurityContext, and admission controls—essential skills for securing containerized workloads.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped RBAC**: Role and RoleBinding for resource access control within specific namespaces
- **ServiceAccount isolation**: Dedicated service accounts to separate pod identities and permissions
- **PodSecurityContext**: Security constraints including runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping
- **Admission controls**: PodSecurity standards and OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement at admission time

## Code Example

```yaml
# ServiceAccount (dev)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
---
# Role for read-only access to ConfigMaps and Secrets
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: data-processor-role
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
# RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: data-processor-binding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: data-processor-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test the RBAC permissions locally?
- What changes are needed for the prod namespace?
- How would you implement network policies alongside these security controls?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests a candidate's ability to enforce governance rules on Kubernetes manifests via CI, start with beginner checks, and wire local + CI verification.

## Key Concepts

- PodDisruptionBudget basics
- Pod security via readOnlyRootFilesystem
- GitHub Actions workflow basics
- local kubectl dry-run validation

## Code Example

```yaml
# failing manifest (no PDB, readOnlyRootFilesystem: false)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: svc-a
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-reg/app-a:latest
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

```yaml
# passing manifest (PDB + readOnlyRootFilesystem: true)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: svc-a
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: my-reg/app-a@sha256:abc
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: pdb-svc-a
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: svc-a
```

```yaml
# GitHub Actions gate (minimal)
name: PDB + ReadOnlyRootFilesystem gate
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  ck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'latest'
      - name: Lint manifests
        run: |
          kubectl version --client
          echo 'Lint step placeholder for yamllint/jsonlint'
      - name: Validate PDB and readOnlyRootFilesystem
        run: |
          # simple validation example
          if ! kubectl get pdb pdb-svc-a >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo 'PDB missing for svc-a'; exit 1
          fi
          if ! grep -R "readOnlyRootFilesystem: true" -n k8s || true; then
            echo 'Some container not enforcing readOnlyRootFilesystem'; exit 1
          fi
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale this gate to cover all namespaces and workloads beyond Deployments? 
- What are the trade-offs of enforcing readOnlyRootFilesystem strictly vs allowing certain privileged ops for debugging?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests the ability to combine SBOM provenance, cryptographic attestation, and admission control in multi-tenant Kubernetes environments with concrete artifacts and workflow.

## Key Concepts
- SBOM provenance (CycloneDX)
- Cosign signatures and Rekor attestations
- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Rego policy validation for image attestation and CVE severity

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: ImageSBOMAttestation
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: ImageSBOMAttestation
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package imagesbomattestation
      
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.object.metadata.namespace != "monitoring"
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        not valid_image(container.image)
        msg := sprintf("Container image %v fails SBOM/attestation validation", [container.image])
      }
      
      valid_image(image) {
        has_attestation(image)
        no_high_severity_vulns(image)
      }
```

## Code Example

```javascript
// OPA Rego (conceptual)
package kubernetes.admission
violation[reason] {
  input.review.object.kind == "Pod"
  image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
  not imageIsAttested(image)
  reason = "image provenance missing"
}
```

```javascript
// Kyverno policy (conceptual)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-provenance-and-security
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-nonroot
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "must set runAsNonRoot and readOnlyRootFilesystem"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:

    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "image must have Rekor cosign attestation"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "*attested*"
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests foundational secure supply chain practices in a beginner-friendly manner. It mirrors real-world CI gates used in production environments around Dockerfile hygiene, image signing, SBOM generation, and registry controls. It introduces modern tools like Cosign and SBOM attestations without overwhelming complexity.

## Key Concepts

- **Dockerfile Hygiene**: Non-root USER and multi-stage builds reduce security vulnerabilities and image size
- **Container Image Signing**: Using Cosign to sign and verify container images ensures integrity
- **SBOM Attestation**: Software Bill of Materials provides transparency into image contents and dependencies
- **GitHub Actions Workflows**: Implementing gates and policy checks in CI/CD pipelines
- **Registry Allowlist**: Restricting deployments to approved registries prevents supply chain attacks

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow
name: Docker Security Gate
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Validate Dockerfile
        run: |
          # Check for non-root USER
          grep -q 'USER ' Dockerfile || exit 1
          # Check for multi-stage build
          grep -q 'FROM.*AS' Dockerfile || exit 1
      
      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: |
          syft ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }} -o spdx-json > sbom.json
      
      - name: Sign image and SBOM with Cosign
        run: |
          cosign sign ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cosign attest --type spdx-json --predicate sbom.json ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
      
      - name: Verify signature and attestation
        run: |
          cosign verify ${{ vars.REGISTRY }}/app:${{ github.sha }}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests the ability to enforce Kubernetes scheduling best practices through automated CI gates. It demonstrates understanding of pod distribution for high availability, GitOps workflows, and infrastructure-as-code validation.

## Key Concepts

- **Kubernetes topologySpreadConstraints**: Controls how pods are distributed across failure domains (zones, nodes, etc.)
- **Deployment replicas and scaling**: Understanding when and why to distribute workloads
- **YAML parsing in CI pipelines**: Using Python or Node.js to validate manifests
- **GitHub Actions workflow configuration**: Building automated gates for GitOps
- **Local validation and pre-commit hooks**: Catching issues before code reaches CI

## Code Example

```python
# gate-topology.py
import sys
import yaml
import glob

def check_deploymentConstraints(doc):
    if doc.get('kind') != 'Deployment':
        return True
    
    replicas = doc.get('spec', {}).get('replicas', 1)
    if replicas <= 2:
        return True
    
    topology = doc.get('spec', {}).get('template', {}).get('spec', {})
    if 'topologySpreadConstraints' not in topology:
        return False
    
    for constraint in topology['topologySpreadConstraints']:
        if constraint.get('topologyKey') != 'topology.kubernetes.io/zone':
            return False
        maxSkew = constraint.get('maxSkew', 1)
        if maxSkew > 1:
            return False
    
    return True

def main():
    failed = []
    for manifest in glob.glob('**/*.yaml', recursive=True):
        with open(manifest) as f:
            docs = yaml.safe_load_all(f)
            for doc in docs:
                if doc and not check_deploymentConstraints(doc):
                    failed.append(manifest)
    
    if failed:
        print(f"Failing manifests: {failed}")
        sys.exit(1)
    
    print("All Deployments pass topology constraints check")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

## GitHub Actions Workflow

```yaml
name: Topology Constraints Gate
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  enforce-topology:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install pyyaml
      - name: Run topology gate
        run: python gate-topology.py
```

## Failing Manifest Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Passing Manifest Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
      - maxSkew: 1
        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
        whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: web
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:latest
```

## How to Verify

**Local Verification:**
```bash
pip install pyyaml
python gate-topology.py
```

**CI Verification:**
The GitHub Actions workflow runs automatically on pull requests. Merges are blocked until all Deployments with replicas > 2 include proper topologySpreadConstraints.

**Pre-commit Hook:**
Add to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:
```yaml
repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: topology-gate
        name: Enforce topologySpreadConstraints
        entry: python gate-topology.py
        language: system
        types: [yaml]
```

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for ns in $(kubectl get ns -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  kubectl -n "$ns" get resourcequota >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing ResourceQuota in $ns"; exit 1; }
  kubectl -n "$ns" get limitrange >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "Missing LimitRange in $ns"; exit 1; }
  for dep in $(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {/end}'); do
    sa=$(kubectl -n "$ns" get deploy "$dep" -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName}')

    kubectl -n "$ns" get rolebinding | grep -q "$sa" || { echo "Missing RBAC for $sa in $ns"; exit 1; }
  done
done
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests basic understanding of Kubernetes security posture and practical gate design in CI, covering both Pod security and NetworkPolicy defaults.

## Key Concepts
- Pod securityContext and container.securityContext
- Kyverno vs OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement
- Default-deny NetworkPolicy per Namespace
- Local validation with kubectl and kyverno/opa tooling
- CI validation with GitHub Actions hooks

## Code Example
```yaml
# Kyverno ClusterPolicy (minimal)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-secctx
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-security-context
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must set readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and runAsNonRoot: true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
              runAsNonRoot: true
              allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
```

```yaml
# NetworkPolicy default-deny (Namespace scope)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt the policy to exclude specific namespaces or namespaces with legacy workloads?
- How would you test this in a multi-tenant CI environment with limited cluster access?
